definition: The passage of institutions, property or concepts from the religious to the profane domain. The word comes from canon law (the religious who returns to the world) and from the treaties of Westphalia (Church property transferred to princes), before coming to designate, in the nineteenth century, the retreat of religion in modern societies. The debate that Part Eleven puts on trial concerns its nature: a transposition of Christian contents, for Schmitt (the concepts of the State) and Löwith (eschatology become philosophy of history); a category of historical injustice, for Blumenberg, who sets against it the reoccupation of empty places by new answers; an exit from religion produced by Christianity itself, for Gauchet; the passage of belief to one option among others, for Taylor; a translation of religious contents, for Habermas. Weber had described its mainspring under the name of disenchantment. What the essay retains from the quarrel is that all of them speak of the institution and none of what the individual lives, and that Norris and Inglehart provide the empirical arbitration: it is not critique that secularizes, it is existential security. See also reoccupation, secularized eschatology, disenchantment of the world.

Eschatology is the doctrine of the last things, from the Greek *eschata*: the end of time, judgement, salvation. Karl Löwith's thesis (*Meaning in History*, 1949) is that the modern philosophies of history, from Voltaire and Condorcet to Hegel, Marx and Comte, are Christian eschatology transposed: history oriented towards a goal, progress, revolution, the positive state, inherits the Jewish and Christian expectation of salvation, and historical materialism is a messianism in the language of political economy; Comte takes up the three ages of Joachim of Fiore. The Greeks, who thought of time as a cycle, had no philosophy of history. Löwith concludes in favour of a Stoic withdrawal, for which Habermas reproaches him in 1963. Blumenberg answers him that identity of function does not prove identity of content (attested response). The essay holds Löwith to be an ambiguous ally: the best historical support for its thesis, who refounds nothing but proposes no way of living; it judges that its criterion owes more to Stirner than to Löwith. See also secularization, reoccupation.

Hans Blumenberg's concept (*Die Legitimität der Neuzeit*, 1966) against the thesis of secularization, which he holds to be a category of historical injustice: modernity does not inherit Christian contents, it occupies with new answers places, questions, that theology had opened and then left empty, such as that of the meaning of history. Identity of function creates the appearance of a historical identity that is mere semblance. Modernity is a self-assertion (*Selbstbehauptung*) of man against the theological absolutism of the late Middle Ages, the arbitrary God of nominalism. Blumenberg thereby answers Löwith and Schmitt (attested responses). The essay makes it the second great objection to its thesis, symmetrical to Durkheim's: to see a religion wherever a place is occupied would be an optical illusion, and the extensive version of the thesis proves too much. It concedes the point, and makes its criterion the answer: secular religion in Aron's sense distinguishes modest reoccupations from reoccupations by a sacrificial absolute. Blumenberg is an unexpected ally, in the order of history. See also secularization, secularized eschatology.

Raymond Aron's expression (*L'avenir des religions séculières*, 1944, paraphrased by the essay), close to Eric Voegelin's political religions (*Die politischen Religionen*, 1938), for the doctrines that take the place of vanished faith in people's souls and situate salvation here below, in the future of humanity: communism and Nazism first and foremost, the deified *Volk*, History as judge. Voegelin gives them a genealogy, gnosis, the immanentization of the eschaton since Joachim of Fiore; Aron keeps to the function. Kelsen objects to Voegelin that his is a theory that proves everything (attested response), and Blumenberg sees in it a second victory over gnosis. The essay sides with Kelsen and Blumenberg against the genealogy, and against them on the function: secular religion in Aron's sense is indispensable to it, because it neutralizes the crossed objections of Durkheim and Blumenberg. The secular religions of the twentieth century are the most massive cases of the sacrifice criterion, and appear in the conclusion among the strict refoundations. See also sacrifice criterion, reoccupation.

In Habermas (*Glauben und Wissen*, acceptance speech for the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade, Frankfurt, 14 October 2001), the condition of secularized societies that must reckon lastingly with the presence of religious communities and with their resources of meaning. Reciprocity is required on both sides: believers accept that public authority be neutral, unbelievers do not hold religion to be a mere archaism. Public reason has the task of translating religious contents rather than liquidating them: a secularization that does not annihilate is accomplished in the mode of translation, as the image of man created in the image of God (Gn 1, 27) has become the equal dignity of all, and Kant is the first example of a secularizing and saving deconstruction. The essay sees in it a third way between Löwith and Blumenberg, but remarks that Habermas translates only normative contents and does not say how the individual lives without religion. The essay has not read the debate with Ratzinger (2004). See also secularization.

In Pierre Hadot (*Exercices spirituels et philosophie antique*, 1981), the practices by which the ancient schools, Stoics, Epicureans, Platonists, transformed the way of seeing and being of their members: attention to oneself, examination of conscience, meditation on death, premeditation of evils, the view from above, concentration on the present. Philosophy there is a way of life before being a discourse. The word comes from Ignatius of Loyola, the thing from the philosophers: it is a debt reversed, and the Christian exercises inherited the ancient ones. Hadot reproaches Foucault, who takes up these themes in the care of the self, with an aesthetics of existence too close to dandyism, because it forgets that the sage places himself in the perspective of the Whole (attested response). The essay finds in Hadot the most exact historical description of the spirituality of exercise that it proposes in answer to its question, with Spinoza for the ontology and Wittgenstein for the limit: the Whole there is a horizon of lucidity, not an object of adoration. Hadot figures among the exceptions, in the position of immanence. See also spirituality.

In Karl Jaspers (*Der philosophische Glaube*, 1948; *Der philosophische Glaube angesichts der Offenbarung*, 1962), a faith without revelation or Church: the relation to transcendence that philosophy experiences without being able to know it, which gives itself in ciphers, the language of transcendence, and in limit situations, and which no orthodoxy can possess. It refuses to let any revelation be exclusive, and reads the Trinity and Christ themselves as ciphers of human possibilities. Barth reproaches it with a transcendence without content; Bultmann, with an untranslated myth, to which Jaspers replies that myth cannot be translated without loss; Camus, in *The Myth of Sisyphus*, with philosophical suicide, the leap by which the absurd becomes god (attested responses). The essay judges Camus right in logic but not with regard to its criterion, since Jaspers's leap ends in no obedience, and it compares Jaspers to Heidegger: the same structure of expectation, but communication saves him. Jaspers is a cautious believing exception, with a reservation about the inflation of ciphers. See also limit situations, Encompassing.

In Jaspers (*Psychologie der Weltanschauungen*, 1919; *Philosophie*, 1932), the situations one can neither change nor avoid, and against which one can only collide as against a wall: death, suffering, struggle, guilt, and the very fact of always being in a situation. They are not resolved, they are lived; existence experiences itself in them, and it is in them, in failure (*Scheitern*), that transcendence makes itself felt, without ever becoming an object. They are, with ciphers and communication, one of the paths of philosophical faith. Camus, who reads Jaspers in *The Myth of Sisyphus*, starts from the same experience of the absurd and refuses the leap; the essay notes that the two attitudes part on the answer, not on the ordeal. Limit situations can be compared with helplessness in Freud and with death as the source of religion in Malinowski, but Jaspers draws from them no explanation of belief: he sees in them an opening, not a need. See also philosophical faith, Encompassing.

In Jaspers (*Vernunft und Existenz*, 1935; *Von der Wahrheit*, 1947), that which envelops every horizon without being able to become an object: being itself, which neither subject nor object exhausts, and within which all knowledge stands. The Encompassing presents itself in several modes, empirical existence, consciousness in general, spirit, existence proper, the world and transcendence; none can be grasped from outside, and every thought that believes it holds it misses it. Ciphers are the language by which transcendence, the Encompassing of all Encompassings, makes itself heard without giving itself up. The notion brings Jaspers close to negative theology, from Plotinus to Eckhart, and to the mystical in Wittgenstein, for whom it is not how the world is that is mystical, but that it is; the essay counts these three attitudes among the refusals to let an answer occupy the place of the question. See also philosophical faith, limit situations, negative theology.

The question whether believing is subject to duties. William Clifford (*The Ethics of Belief*, 1877) maintains, with the example of the shipowner who silences his doubts about his ship, that “it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence”. William James (*The Will to Believe*, 1896) replies that one has the right to believe, at one's own risk, when the option is living, forced and momentous, and reason cannot decide: dupery for dupery, nothing proves that dupery through hope is worse than dupery through fear, and the duty to shun error is not the only one, there is also that of seeking truth. Russell, Mackie and Plantinga extend the debate. The essay combines the two: one has the right to believe where reason leaves the question open, and this right ceases where belief engages the lives of others without their having chosen it, which is the translation of the sacrifice criterion into the order of knowledge, and holds against the Inquisitor as against crusades waged in Clifford's name. See also sacrifice criterion, Grand Inquisitor.

The name the essay gives to a regularity observed over two centuries: each critique of religion is accused by the next of having remained religious. Stirner reproaches Feuerbach with it, Marx Stirner, Nietzsche all the atheists of his time, Heidegger Nietzsche, Camus Marx, and Onfray, according to a reported formula, Comte-Sponville. The accusation is always the same: you think you have left religion, but you are still in it. It was Stirner who first formulated it, in 1844, in the sentence the essay takes as its guiding thread, “Unsere Atheisten sind fromme Leute”, our atheists are pious people; for this reason the essay also calls it Stirner's law, and notes that Stirner did not escape it himself, since he puts the Ego in the place of God. The full text speaks of a regularity that ends up resembling a law; the assessment in the conclusion draws up its list and shows why it is no accident: the place left empty by God answers a need for meaning, connection and protection that critique does not abolish. See also Sacrifice criterion, Strict refoundation and soft refoundation, Pious atheists.

The two degrees of the sacrifice criterion. Refoundation in the strict sense installs an absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded and whose critique becomes a sacrilege: Plato's law, Rousseau's civil religion, Comte's Great Being, the secular religions of the twentieth century, the History of the revolutionaries that Camus denounces, Schmitt's political theology. Soft refoundation contents itself with the need to consecrate: it declares human realities sacred, love, the relation of I and Thou, freedom, without demanding of anyone that he die for them. The essay finds its textbook case in Feuerbach, whom Engels reproached in 1886 with wanting to complete religion rather than abolish it, and its most liberal form in Luc Ferry. The distinction matters because the soft prepares the strict: it is through the need to consecrate that consecration becomes a demand among the successors, and the essay sees in Onfray the case of an author who has taken the step, his Civilization demanding that one defend a liturgy in which one does not believe. See also Sacrifice criterion, Self-offering, Law of refoundations.

The essay's rule of method, announced in the prologue and recalled at each encounter between two authors. An attested response is a debate that took place: one of the two read the other and answered him, in a text that can be quoted, as Origen against Celsus, Pascal against Montaigne, Feuerbach against Stirner, Freud against Rolland, Blumenberg against Löwith. A constructed confrontation is a face-to-face that the essay itself organizes between authors who did not read each other or did not answer each other: Plato and Rousseau, Maimonides and Feuerbach, Bayle and Ivan Karamazov, Wittgenstein and Leibniz. The essay signals the status of each exchange so as not to pass off a reconstruction as a historical fact. The sections entitled “constructed debate” (morality without God, why do people believe, why something rather than nothing) are constructed confrontations for several voices. The site's Responses page lists the seventy-two exchanges, fifty-eight attested and fourteen constructed, with their section. See also Eight regimes of critique.

The narrative the prologue sets out to undo: that of a critique of religion handed on like a torch, from Lucretius to Spinoza, from the Enlightenment to Feuerbach, from Marx to Nietzsche and Freud, each runner taking the baton from the one before until atheism is complete. The essay sets three findings against it. The critiques do not aim at the same thing: error, symptom, value, illusion, function are not a single adversary under different names. They accuse one another instead of completing one another, which is the subject of the law of refoundations. Finally, the harshest critique of religion often comes from inside faith, in Pascal, Kierkegaard, Barth or Simone Weil, whom the fable ignores. The prologue adds that Christianity did not forge the weapons of its critique alone, and that to forget this would be to perpetuate the fable, hence the place given to Averroes, Maimonides, Arkoun and Bidar. See also Eight regimes of critique, Law of refoundations.

The unbelievers who surround the madman of § 125 of *The Gay Science* (1882), the one who runs into the marketplace with a lantern crying that he is looking for God. They mock him, and it is to them, not to believers, that he announces that we have killed him, you and I. The essay makes them a type: the atheists of the marketplace take the absence of God for a settled matter, one more opinion, whereas the madman knows that it is an event whose consequences have not yet been measured, and which calls for festivals of atonement and sacred games. The essay places among them the new atheists of the early twenty-first century, Dawkins, Harris, Dennett, Hitchens, Sartre in his own way, and those who believe they find in meditation a wisdom without history and without presuppositions: all of them carry shadows they do not see. The figure says, in Nietzschean terms, what the law of refoundations says in Stirnerian terms. See also Death of God, Law of refoundations, Nihilism.

The role the essay assigns to Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor. Dostoevsky does not argue, he embodies; the figure he invents shows what becomes of a religion from which God has been removed and which keeps miracle, mystery and authority, for the happiness of a humanity judged incapable of freedom. The essay uses it as a touchstone, that is, as the test to which it submits the other authors: Voltaire wrote its programme a century earlier, in the Epistle to the Author of the Three Impostors; Comte is its believing version, founding a Church without God; Demopheles, in Schopenhauer's dialogue, the version without tragedy; Onfray, who defends the Latin Mass without believing in it, the contemporary case. The touchstone also holds in the order of knowledge: for Russell as reread by the essay, the problem is not belief, it is the Inquisitor. See also Grand Inquisitor, Sacrifice criterion.

The form taken, according to the conclusion, by an exit from religion that does not refound another: not a doctrine but a practice by which the subject transforms himself in order to gain access to the true, in the sense Foucault gives to spirituality and that Hadot describes among the Ancients. The essay finds its most coherent ontology in Spinoza, its most exact historical description in Hadot, its strictest limit in Wittgenstein, and neighbouring forms in Nietzsche, Camus or Murdoch. Three traits distinguish it from a religion in the strong sense: it knows where it comes from, it installs no absolute that demands the sacrifice of others, it is a way of living rather than a system. Yet it keeps, knowingly, an orientation towards a Whole or a Good that it does not possess. The essay recalls that it also has a Christian genealogy, through Augustine's inwardness, and that it presupposes an existential security that only institutions guarantee. See also Spirituality, Spiritual exercises, Wonder without debt.

The clause that, in the final formulation of the sacrifice criterion, settles the borderline cases. What refounds a religion is not that a man agrees to die for what he loves, but that an authority demands this devotion of others and treats its critique as sacrilege. Justin dying for having refused a cult, Clifford's scientist who renounces a consolation, Ferry's man ready to die for freedom found nothing: freely consented self-offering does not fall under the criterion. Rome demanding Justin's sacrifice, the Grand Inquisitor, Rousseau's civil religion punishing with death whoever lies before the laws, do fall under it. The distinction allows the essay not to condemn every absolute, but only the absolute that has priests to speak in its name and victims to designate, and to leave Ferry the rank of soft rather than strict refounder. See also Sacrifice criterion, Strict refoundation and soft refoundation, Victimary mechanism.

The title of the last section of the conclusion and the question it leaves open. Marx, in the Introduction of 1844, does not say only that religion is the opium of the people: it is also the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, the Protestation against real misery. If religion were only an error, its disappearance would be pure gain; if it is also a lament, what becomes of this lament when heaven empties? The essay judges that the wisdoms of immanence answer it badly: Spinoza before Ivan Karamazov, Comte-Sponville before Hausemer, console for injustice by making it understood. Bonhoeffer and Simone Weil, believers, withdraw the opium without withdrawing the protest. For the unbeliever, the most just answer is Camus's, “Je me révolte, donc nous sommes”, I rebel, therefore we are: the lament changes its address and turns towards other human beings, on condition that this we remain horizontal, never become a god and never designate a victim. See also Opium of the people, Protestation, Revolt.

The distinction that opens Part Nine, devoted to the causes of belief. To speak of a religious need, as Durkheim does, and as Feuerbach's formulas on desire and Freud's on helplessness incline one to do, is to suppose a constant lack that demands to be filled, and that will be filled by a substitute if religion disappears; to speak of a disposition is to designate something in the human mind that makes gods easy to think and belief probable, without making it a necessity. The essay chooses the second word and asks anthropologists, psychologists, sociologists and the cognitive sciences what the religious disposition owes to fear, to desire, to society, to death and to the very structure of the mind. The constructed debate that closes the part concludes that the disposition is universal in its springs and variable in its intensity: there is a need for meaning, connection and protection, not a need for God, and this is why exits from religion are costly exceptions, which presuppose wisdom and security. See also Existential security, Minimally counterintuitive concepts, Illusion.

The affect that the essay retains, at the end of the constructed debate on Leibniz's question, as the only religious affect that demands nothing. To wonder that there is something rather than nothing is the beginning of philosophy in Plato and Aristotle and, in Wittgenstein, the mystical itself: not how the world is, but that it is. The essay distinguishes four treatments of the question: the demand that leads to God (Leibniz, Schelling), dissolution (Hume, Kant in his way, Bergson, Carnap, the Wittgenstein of 6.5), wonder without an answer (Plato, Aristotle, the Wittgenstein of 6.44, Jaspers) and debt (Heidegger, for whom wonder becomes sacrifice). The danger is to transform the fact into a gift: a gift calls for gratitude, gratitude for a creditor, and the creditor, sooner or later, for a sacrifice. Wonder without debt founds no obligation, promises nothing, has neither addressee to thank nor altar on which to sacrifice; to think being is not to owe it something. It is the barest affect of the spirituality of exercise. See also Spirituality of exercise, Principle of sufficient reason, Onto-theology.

The expression comes from Pascal's Memorial, dated 23 November 1654: “Dieu d'Abraham, Dieu d'Isaac, Dieu de Jacob, non des philosophes et des savants”, God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars. It designates the God that reason demonstrates and needs in order to ground the world: Aristotle's first mover, Plotinus's One, the simple and immutable Being of Augustine and Anselm, cause of itself and guarantor of eternal truths in Descartes, necessary substance in Leibniz. The essay shows that this God was born of a fusion, that of Plato's God and the God of the Bible, accomplished by Philo, Justin and Augustine, and that he is the major fact of the intellectual history of the Christian West. The moderns undo him from two sides: Pascal from above, by setting against him the God of a history and a revelation; Heidegger from below, by showing that the causa sui has nothing divine about it, that one can neither pray to it nor dance before it. Spinoza kept him while withdrawing everything the Bible had given him. See also Onto-theology, Causa sui, First mover and thinking of thinking.

Nietzsche's formula in the preface to *Beyond Good and Evil* (1886): Christianity is Platonism for the people, “Christenthum ist Platonismus für's Volk”. It reverses, while keeping it, the reproach of Tertullian, who asked around 200 what Athens has in common with Jerusalem and denounced a Stoic, Platonic and dialectical Christianity. The essay takes it as the thread of its Part Two: the formula is a polemic, but it designates a fact that historians do not dispute, Christianity thought itself in the categories of Greek philosophy, beginning with that of Logos, from Philo and Justin to Augustine. The elitist reading it presupposes, a philosophical truth translated into images for the multitude, itself has a long history, from Aristotle to Averroes and Schopenhauer. Heidegger will take up the phrase in another sense, to say that Western philosophy, understood as Platonism, has reached its end. See also Logos, Double truth, Allegory.

The shortest name the essay gives to what the sacrifice criterion detects: an absolute, whatever its name, God, the city, Humanity, History, Race, Civilization, in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded and whose critique becomes a sacrilege. The expression serves above all to decide between modern reoccupations. Blumenberg is right to say that not every occupied place is a religion; but among the answers given to the questions theology left behind, some are modest hypotheses and others install a sacrificial absolute, and it is to these alone that secular religion in Aron's sense applies. Justin's martyrdom is not the sacrificial absolute that the criterion denounces, since it is Rome that makes the demand; Comte-Sponville's wisdom refounds none, but risks accepting injustice. The criterion does not condemn every absolute: it condemns the one that demands the sacrifice of others and has priests to speak in its name. See also Sacrifice criterion, Secular religions, Reoccupation.

Περιαγωγή, the turning around. In the allegory of the cave (*Republic* VII, 518c-d), Plato says that education is not the filling of an empty soul, but the art of turning the whole soul, with the organ by which it sees, from what becomes towards what is, like an eye that cannot be turned towards the light without turning the whole body. The essay sees in it the first philosophical name for what Foucault will call spirituality: a transformation of the subject necessary to gain access to the true, whose end is the Good situated beyond essence (509b). The figure returns under the name of conversion of the gaze: in Zosima, who answers Ivan's evil not with an argument but with a change of vision; in Murdoch, for whom moral life is a conversion of attention that turns away from the self towards the Good. It brings out the two Platos whose tension runs through the essay, the legislator of the *Laws* and the Plato of conversion, and it is the second that the spiritualities without God claim. See also Spirituality, Spiritual exercises, Unselfing.

Σωφρονιστήριον, the house where one is made wise. In Book X of the *Laws* (908a-909a), having proved the gods exist through the self-moving soul, Plato provides three prisons in his city; this one, next to the seat of the nocturnal council, is intended for the impious man of good faith, who denies the gods from want of judgement, not from vice. He will spend at least five years there, visited only by members of the council, who come to instruct him; if he relapses on release, he will be put to death. The essay stresses that this is a forced school, not a place of torture, that the impious man is treated as sick in soul, and that the religion imposed on him is a rational theology, not that of the poets. This is precisely what makes the *Laws* the pure case of the sacrifice criterion: once truth has been demonstrated, it can be demanded, and its critique becomes a crime. Popper made it the first enemy of the open society; the essay sees in it the original of which almost all later refoundations are copies, and the ancestor of the Grand Inquisitor. See also Sacrifice criterion, Grand Inquisitor, Civil religion.

fr: Premier moteur et pensée de la pensée
terme: First mover and thinking of thinking
definition: The two determinations of Aristotle's god in Book Λ of the *Metaphysics*. The eternal movement of the heavens requires a first mover that is not itself moved, otherwise there would be an infinite regress; now what moves without being moved is the object of desire: the first mover moves as what is loved (Λ 7). This god is pure act, and its activity can only be the highest: it thinks itself, and its thinking is thinking of thinking, νόησις νοήσεως (Λ 9, 1074b34). It is therefore ignorant of the world, did not create it and does not care for it, which is Plato's second impiety. The essay shows the paradox of its posterity: this indifferent god became the God of the philosophers of the three monotheisms, through Averroes, Maimonides and Thomas Aquinas, and the definition of first philosophy as theological science (E 1) is the source of what Heidegger will call onto-theology. Aristotle himself attaches no cult to it; the contemplative life of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, to make oneself immortal as far as possible, is an exercise without religion. See also God of the philosophers, Onto-theology, Causa sui.

Ἀταραξία, the absence of disturbance. In Epicurus and Lucretius, knowledge of nature is not an end in itself: it is an exercise that delivers from the two fears that spoil life, fear of the gods and fear of death, and procures tranquillity of soul. Explaining lightning, earthquakes and disease by atoms dispels terror; knowing that death is nothing to us, since where it is we no longer are, dispels the other. The essay insists on this spiritual dimension of the regime of error, which the moderns will forget: Epicurus is not an atheist, the gods exist and live in a blessedness that any care would disturb, and the impious man is the one who lends them the opinions of the crowd. This is why the essay says of Onfray, who claims Epicurus and Lucretius, that he inherits from them the regime of error and the hatred of priests, not their piety or their exercise. Ataraxia is the ancestor of the wisdoms of immanence that Part Twelve examines. See also Spiritual exercises, Spirituality of exercise, Eight regimes of critique.

The interpretation that leads a word back to what it truly signifies. In *The Decisive Treatise* (*Faṣl al-maqāl*), Averroes lays down that truth cannot be contrary to truth: if a demonstration arrives at a knowledge that the apparent meaning (*ẓāhir*) of the revealed text contradicts, the text must be interpreted and brought back to its inner meaning (*bāṭin*) by taʾwīl. Demonstration never bends; the text does. Then arises the question of the addressee: to whom should the true meaning be told? Averroes answers with an anthropology of assent, the people of demonstration, the people of dialectic and the people of rhetoric, and forbids divulging interpretations to the common people. The essay concludes that Averroes does not leave religion and founds nothing: he divides, and demands of the people the sacrifice of access to the true, a solution taken up, under other names, by Spinoza, Comte, Renan and Leo Strauss. The legend of a double truth, born of the condemnations of 1277, distorts this position, which knows only one truth with two levels of access. See also Double truth, Allegory, Art of writing.

Detachment, letting-be, the serenity of one who has renounced willing. The word comes from Meister Eckhart, for whom the poverty in spirit of sermon 52 consists in willing nothing, knowing nothing and having nothing, to the point of praying God to be rid of God, that is, of the idol one makes of him. The essay distinguishes two readings: a negative theology pushed to the limit, which aims at the nameless Godhead, and a modern reading that makes Eckhart the ancestor of the spiritualities without God, detachment becoming an exercise in dispossession that no longer needs any object; Schopenhauer will hail in him a brother of the sages of India, Simone Weil will speak of decreation. Heidegger deliberately takes up the word in the small volume *Gelassenheit* (1959) to name a thinking that renounces calculation and holds itself in expectation; the essay sees in it Eckhart displaced, and objects that this expectation without content remains a piety without object. See also Negative theology, Decreation, Spiritual exercises.

The reading that seeks beneath the letter of a sacred text another meaning, philosophical or moral. Philo of Alexandria, in the 1st century, reads Genesis with the *Timaeus*: when the two seem to diverge, it is because the letter of Moses hides a meaning that allegory must uncover, and the Logos is its key. The essay speaks of a regime of allegory, earlier than all the regimes of critique: Philo does not criticize religion, he translates it into philosophy, which protects it from the rationalist objection but installs in it a double meaning, reserved for those who know how to read. The method passes to the Christians through Origen, who systematizes it, and reappears in Averroes and Maimonides, for whom the revealed text has an apparent meaning and an inner meaning. Schopenhauer gives its disillusioned version: religions are the allegorical garment of truth, the metaphysics of the masses, and it would be cruel to take away the people's allegory. The Grand Inquisitor is the political culmination of this reading. See also Logos, Taʾwīl, Double truth, Demythologization.

Λόγος σπερματικός, reason sown. Justin, in the middle of the 2nd century, maintains in his Apologies that the Logos that became incarnate in Christ was always present, in the state of seed, in all human beings: each philosopher spoke well to the extent that he had a share in the seminal Logos, and whatever has been well said among all men belongs to the Christians (2 Apology, 13). Socrates and Heraclitus, who lived according to the Logos, are thus Christians before Christ. The essay notes the double face of the formula: an opening, which recognizes truth outside the Church, and an annexation, which makes Greek wisdom a Christian property and philosophy a preparation. Augustine will repeat the gesture when he debates with the Platonists without excluding that other sages thought the same of God, which the essay calls the politeness of a victor. The word comes from the Stoics, for whom seminal reasons are the rational germs of all things. See also Logos, Platonism for the people, Allegory.

Fragment 233 of the *Pensées* in the Brunschvicg edition, the most famous and, according to the essay, the most misread. Pascal addresses a libertine who can neither believe nor decide: since reason cannot settle the matter, one must wager, and the stake is such, an eternity of happiness against a finite life, that wagering for God is the only reasonable choice. The essay acknowledges that this is a calculation of interest, but maintains that the essential lies elsewhere: to the man who is convinced and still cannot believe, Pascal replies that he should act as if he believed, take holy water and have masses said, and this will make you believe and will stupefy you. Practice precedes belief and produces it, which Durkheim and Hume will each rediscover in their own way. The wager is thus an exercise more than a proof. William James, in *The Will to Believe*, judges it severely: the wager is valid only for one who already has a tendency to believe, and James keeps from Pascal the right of the heart while leaving him the calculation. See also Hidden God, Fideism, Ethics of belief.

Pascal takes up the verse of Isaiah, “Vere tu es Deus absconditus” (Is 45, 15), and makes it a thesis: Scripture says that God is a hidden God (fr. 242). One must therefore not seek to prove him from nature, as the apologists do; nature everywhere marks a lost God, and God gives enough light for those who want to see him, enough obscurity for those who do not. The essay draws from this that the critique of the God of the philosophers comes here from inside faith: Descartes's demonstrated God is useless for salvation, and the true God is the God of a history. The theme then runs through the series. Hegel quotes Pascal's phrase on the lost God to think the death of God; Weber sees in Calvinist Puritanism, which suppresses the sacraments and leaves the believer alone before a hidden God, a stage of disenchantment; Blumenberg dates modern self-assertion from man's answer to a hidden and unpredictable God, that of nominalism; Simone Weil takes up the idea of a God who withdraws. See also God of the philosophers, Pascal's wager, Self-assertion.

God, that is, Nature. The formula appears in the preface to the fourth part of the *Ethics*: the reason, or cause, for which God, that is, Nature, acts and for which he exists is one and the same. The essay stresses that it does not abolish God, it displaces him: God is no longer a person outside the world who creates it, judges it and loves it, but the single substance of which everything that exists is a mode, and which acts by the sole necessity of its nature. Spinoza keeps the name of God out of conviction, not prudence: Novalis will call him a God-intoxicated man, Hegel will say that Spinozism is not an atheism but an acosmism, in which there is too much God and not enough world. The essay makes this position the major exception of its series, the position of immanence: an exit from religion that refounds nothing because it renounces leaving entirely and keeps, knowingly, the name of what it has transformed. Leo Strauss objects that this exception rests on an indemonstrable decision. See also Intellectual love of God, Pantheism and acosmism, Asylum of ignorance.

Amor Dei intellectualis, the summit of the *Ethics*, which hasty readers treat as a rhetorical concession. In proposition 36 of the fifth part, Spinoza writes that the intellectual love of the mind towards God is the very love with which God loves himself. This love is born of knowledge of the third kind, which grasps singular things under the aspect of eternity; it expects nothing in return, since God loves no one in particular, and it is blessedness itself: blessedness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself (V, 42). The essay reads in it a spirituality in Foucault's sense, a transformation of the subject that leads to the true, in a book nonetheless written in geometrical demonstrations, and this is what makes Spinoza the exception par excellence, with Hadot. It recalls that Descartes had already joined knowledge of God to joy, and that Spinoza welds the two ends together. Leo Strauss suspects that Spinoza's apparent piety is partly an art of writing; the essay answers that intellectual love is demonstrated there, not suggested. See also Deus seu Natura, Spirituality of exercise, Oceanic feeling.

Asylum ignorantiae. In the appendix to the first part of the *Ethics*, Spinoza explains the birth of superstition by the finalist prejudice: human beings, who are ignorant of causes and desire what is useful, believe that everything is made for them by gods who govern them, and when an event contradicts this belief, a storm, an earthquake, a disease, they go back from cause to cause until they take refuge in the will of God, that is, the asylum of ignorance. The word thus designates the point where explanation stops to make way for a mystery. The essay makes it the emblem of the regime of error in its most rigorous version: religion as ignorance of causes, a theme d'Holbach will take up in saying that ignorance begets the gods, and that Boyer will rediscover, in another form, by showing how the mind lends intentions where there are only causes. The essay also notes the limit of this explanation: it says why one is mistaken, not why one needs to be mistaken, which Feuerbach, Marx and Freud will seek. See also Deus seu Natura, Eight regimes of critique, Illusion.
